blocks.title: Lecture 7: How the Novel Found Its Readers
paras: **So**, where does the novel come from? **Well**, it depends whom you ask. Some **point to** Cervantes, whose *Don Quixote* appeared in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, and **made fun of** the old chivalric romances. Others **look to** the eighteenth century, **when** Defoe’s *Robinson Crusoe* (1719) and Richardson’s *Pamela* (1740) gave ordinary lives **a serious page**.

**Now**, why **then**? **Three things came together**: a **growing** reading public, **cheaper** printing, and a **middle class** with **leisure** and **a taste for** stories about people like itself. **Let me stress that last point.** The novel was **less a sudden invention than a slow convergence**. **Next week**: how the Victorians **serialised** it. **Questions?**

items.q: Don Quixote appeared in two parts.
The lecturer says the novel was a sudden invention.
items.why: less a sudden invention than a slow convergence.

items.q: The next lecture will be about the Victorians.

blocks.body: Em aulas de história literária, use **datas** e **marcadores de periodização** (*in the eighteenth century, when…*). A estrutura **less X than Y** significa “mais Y do que X”.
*Less a sudden invention than a slow convergence* ≠ *less than*. O *a* repete-se: *less a… than a…*.

items.s: Some ___ to Cervantes as the origin. (point)
It was less a sudden invention ___ a slow convergence. (than)

blocks.title: Match the word to its meaning

items.ans: Where does the novel really begin

body: **Less a… than a…** — Menos um… do que um…
**Mark a turning point.** — Marcar um ponto de virada.
**Where does the novel really begin?** — Onde o romance realmente começa?
**Some point to Cervantes; others look to Defoe.** — Alguns apontam Cervantes; outros olham para Defoe.
